subject: Social Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: What Is a Barter System? Mapping Early Exchange
materials: Printed or hand-drawn images of cowrie shells, Rai stones, Tajadero, Tevau
periods.visual_aids: Display of images: Rai stone disc (Yap), Aztec Tajadero copper knife, Solomon Islands Tevau feather coil, cowrie shells

time_bands.activity: Pose the opening question: 'If there were no money today, how would you get a pencil if all you had was an eraser?' Students individually write two or three sentences on their index card describing the exchange they would arrange. Three or four students share aloud, and the teacher draws out the implicit logic of trading goods for goods.

Teacher displays the images of cowrie shells, Rai stone discs, the Aztec Tajadero, and Tevau feather coils one at a time. For each, students answer: 'What would make this object useful as something to exchange? What would make it difficult?' Pairs discuss and call out reasoning; teacher records key properties — portability, scarcity, recognisability — on the board beside each image.

Teacher defines the barter system ('exchange of goods and services without money') and maps the eraser-for-pencil example onto it. Students then construct a brief written comparison on their index card: choose any two commodity-money objects from the images and explain which one they judge more practical as a medium of exchange and why, citing at least one property recorded on the board.

Three or four pairs share their comparisons. Teacher closes by asking: 'All these objects worked in some communities — what might have changed to make them stop working?' Students propose one idea each; teacher notes responses on the board as a bridge to the problems the barter system creates, which the chapter will explore.

periods.section_context: Cowrie shells, Rai stones, Tajadero, Tevau as early commodity exchange media
periods.teacher_notes: Open with the eraser-pencil scenario to anchor abstract exchange in a tangible, everyday situation students can reason about immediately. A common confusion at this stage is treating barter as simply 'old-fashioned shopping' — push students to notice that no common price standard exists in barter, so every exchange is a fresh negotiation. The commodity-money images from Yap, Mexico, and the Solomon Islands are essential to this unit; source them before the sitting.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare the practical properties of different commodity-exchange objects to evaluate their suitability as media of exchange.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain contributions of Indian and global heritage to living cultural and economic traditions.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify diverse global commodity-money traditions and explain what made each culturally specific.

periods.activity_title: The Farmer's Dilemma: Diagnosing Barter's Limitations
periods.section_anchor: Why Do We Need Money? — Problems of the Barter System
materials: Printed scenario card: 'Farmer with an ox needs shoes, a sweater, and medicines'
A3 paper or notebook page for group diagram

time_bands.activity: Distribute the scenario card. Read it aloud: a farmer owns one ox and needs shoes, a sweater, and medicines. Ask students: 'List every practical problem you can imagine this farmer faces in getting all three items through barter.' Individuals write their list silently for three minutes, then share with a neighbour.

Teacher introduces the five named problems one at a time, using the farmer scenario as the running illustration: (1) double coincidence of wants — the farmer must find someone who wants an ox AND has shoes; (2) no common measure of value — an ox for a pair of shoes is not a proportional exchange; (3) divisibility — the ox cannot be split to buy three separate small items; (4) portability — moving a live ox from place to place is impractical; (5) durability — wheat offered as intermediate payment rots or is eaten by pests. After each problem, pause and ask students where it appeared in their own lists.

Groups of three or four construct a cause-effect diagram on A3 paper: the farmer's ox at the centre; five branches, each labelled with one problem and one concrete consequence drawn from the scenario. Groups must use the textbook terms (double coincidence of wants, measure of value, divisibility, portability, durability) as branch labels.

Two groups display and explain their diagrams. Class compares: did any group add a sixth consequence not on the scenario card? Teacher facilitates a brief discussion on which of the five problems would be most crippling for large-scale trade, requiring students to give a reason for their choice.

periods.section_context: Farmer-ox scenario illustrating double coincidence, measure of value, divisibility, portability, durability
periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently conflate 'double coincidence of wants' with simple scarcity — clarify that the problem is finding two matching needs simultaneously, not merely finding a willing trader. The five problems are distinct and carry specific vocabulary the chapter uses consistently; insist on the correct term for each branch in the diagram. This unit stands on the farmer scenario alone; no prior activity needs to have occurred.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can diagnose the structural limitations of barter exchange by applying named economic problems to a concrete trade scenario.

periods.activity_title: Barter Still Lives: Investigating the Junbeel Mela and Modern Swaps
periods.section_anchor: Why Do We Need Money? — Continuing Barter Practices
materials: Short printed reading: Junbeel Mela description (100–120 words drawn from chapter)
periods.visual_aids: Sketch map or labelled diagram showing Morigaon district of Assam and the hill communities of Meghalaya

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the sketch map and orients students: the Junbeel Mela takes place at Junbeel, Morigaon district, Assam, and draws hill communities — Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi, Jaintia — from Assam and Meghalaya. Ask: 'What does a three-day fair held since the 15th century tell us about how these communities organised trade before there were roads and currency?' Students write one hypothesis on a sticky note.

Students read the printed passage on the Junbeel Mela. After reading, teacher asks three structured questions for whole-class response: (1) What specific goods are exchanged, and why does each side want what the other brings? (2) The fair starts with Agni Puja — what does a ritual opening suggest about the relationship between trade and community in this context? (3) How does the Junbeel Mela avoid the double coincidence problem identified in the previous barter discussion?

Teacher introduces the two modern examples briefly: book exchange clubs (old books for new) and utensil vendors who collect old clothes in exchange for new utensils. Students write on a second sticky note: 'One reason these modern barter examples persist even when money is available.' They place both sticky notes on the board under two columns: 'Junbeel Mela' and 'Modern Swaps'.

Teacher reads aloud the sticky note entries and facilitates a structured discussion: Do the Junbeel Mela and modern swap examples solve the same barter problems in the same way, or different ones? Students must use at least one of the five problem-terms from the farmer scenario. Teacher closes by asking: 'What does the survival of barter tell us about the limits of money as an explanation for everything?'

periods.section_context: Junbeel Mela (Morigaon, Assam), Tiwa–Karbi–Khasi–Jaintia hill trade, book swaps, utensil vendors
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the structural problems of the barter system through the farmer scenario, this unit examines why barter persists — an intellectually distinct question that requires students to think about community, trust, and access rather than efficiency alone. A common confusion is treating the Junbeel Mela as simply a market fair; the chapter emphasises its political and socio-cultural origins alongside its trading function, and both dimensions should be drawn out. Prepare the sketch map before the sitting — Assam and Meghalaya geography is essential context.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse why barter practices persist in specific social and geographic contexts despite the availability of money.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain contributions of Indian and global heritage to living cultural and economic traditions.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how the Junbeel Mela represents a living Indian heritage practice that combines socio-cultural and economic exchange.

periods.activity_title: What Money Does: The Four Functions in Action
materials: Four large cards labelled: Medium of Exchange | Store of Value | Unit of Account | Standard of Deferred Payment
Scenario strips (one set per group of four)

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the four large function cards on the board without explanation. Ask students to predict — in one sentence each — what they think each phrase means. Collect three or four responses per card; do not confirm or correct yet. This surfaces prior knowledge and misconceptions that the teaching will address.

Teacher builds each function explicitly, using the chapter's own illustration for each: (1) Medium of exchange — money replaces the double-coincidence requirement; a shopkeeper accepts it from any buyer. (2) Store of value — money, unlike wheat, does not rot and can be saved for future use. (3) Unit of account — prices provide a single measure that compares the worth of a loaf of bread with the worth of a school fee; the shopkeeper pays workers' salaries, workers buy essentials, the entire loop runs on a common denomination. (4) Standard of deferred payment — a buyer who cannot pay in full today agrees to pay the remainder at a future date, and money is accepted as the means of that future obligation. After each function, return to the student predictions and collectively revise them.

Groups of four receive scenario strips (six short situations — e.g., 'Meena saves ₹200 each month for a new school bag'; 'Ravi pays half the price today and will pay the rest next week'; 'The price tag on a mango and on a book lets you compare their cost'). Groups classify each strip under the correct function card and write one sentence justifying the classification. A function may receive more than one strip.

Groups share classifications; class resolves disagreements. Teacher poses a closing challenge: 'Which single function, if money lost it, would cause the most damage to everyday transactions — and why?' Students write one sentence answer; two or three share aloud.

periods.section_context: Medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account, standard of deferred payment illustrated through shopkeeper–worker cycle
periods.teacher_notes: Students most often conflate 'store of value' with 'savings account' in a modern banking sense — redirect them to the chapter's simpler formulation: money can be set aside and used later without deteriorating, unlike perishable goods. The 'standard of deferred payment' function is the one students find least intuitive; the buyer-pays-later illustration from the chapter is the clearest anchor. The scenario strips should be prepared and cut before the sitting.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply the four functions of money to classify and evaluate real transaction scenarios.

periods.activity_title: Money Through the Ages: Reading India's Monetary Timeline
materials: Printed or hand-drawn blank timeline strip (one per pair): marked 6000 BCE — present
periods.visual_aids: Teacher-drawn master timeline on board: 6000 BCE (barter) → cowrie shells → 1000–600 BCE (metal coins) → 1861 (paper money) → 1980 (debit/credit cards) → 2016 (UPI/digital money)

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the master timeline on the board with six anchor points but initially leaves each label blank. Ask the class: 'What do you already know about how money changed in India?' Students call out any dates or forms they know; teacher places correct ones on the timeline and marks unknown ones with a question mark.

Teacher fills in and explains each anchor point on the master timeline, drawing explicitly on the chapter's sequence: barter exchanges around 6000 BCE; cowrie shells as widely used commodity money; metal coinage emerging between 1000 and 600 BCE; official paper money introduced in India in 1861; debit and credit cards appearing around 1980; UPI and digital money from 2016. For each point, teacher asks: 'What problem did this development solve that the previous form could not?'

Pairs receive their blank timeline strips. Without looking at the board, they reconstruct the six anchor points from memory, add a seventh point of their own choosing (a specific example from within any stage — e.g., kārṣhāpaṇas, Bank of Bengal notes, QR codes), and write one sentence per point explaining the problem it solved. They may then check the master timeline and revise.

Three pairs share their seventh point and its justification. Teacher closes with the Keynes observation the chapter opens with — 'money links the present to the future' — and asks students to place that idea on their timeline: at which point in the sequence does money first genuinely accomplish this linking, and why?

periods.section_context: India's monetary timeline: 6000 BCE barter, cowries, 1000–600 BCE coinage, 1861 paper money, 1980 cards, 2016 UPI
periods.teacher_notes: This unit establishes the chapter's broad chronological spine; students often compress all ancient money into a single undifferentiated past, so the specific dates — particularly the 1000–600 BCE window for coinage and the 1861 introduction of official paper money — deserve deliberate attention. The Keynes framing at the close is not decorative; it sets up the analytical question the coinage and paper money units will answer in concrete historical terms. Prepare the blank timeline strips before the sitting.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can sequence the major stages of monetary evolution and explain the problem each stage resolved.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a chronological account of monetary change and identify the societal problem each transition addressed.

periods.activity_title: Coins as Evidence: Reading Ancient Indian Coinage
materials: Printed coin image sheet: Chalukya Varaha coin, Chola tiger coin, Roman gold coin (Pudukkottai)
Source analysis question card (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Projected or printed images of obverse and reverse of Chalukya coin (Varaha / parasol), Chola silver coin (tiger), Roman gold coin excavated at Pudukkottai

time_bands.activity: Distribute the coin image sheet. Teacher asks: 'A historian finds one of these coins buried in the ground with no label. What can she work out from the object itself?' Students examine the images and note on the source analysis card: (a) what they observe on each coin, (b) one inference they can draw from the observation alone. Share three or four observations aloud.

Teacher builds the vocabulary and historical context: coins in ancient India were called kārṣhāpaṇas or paṇas; the punched symbols were rūpas; minting was the production process and a mint the facility. Explain the obverse/reverse convention and walk through each coin's imagery — the Chalukya Varaha (Vishnu avatar) and three-tiered royal parasol; the Chola tiger on silver; and the Roman gold coins found at Pudukkottai, which scholars read as evidence of India's maritime trade with Rome — trade that, they conclude, favoured India. Connect the word paṇa to its living descendants: paṇaṁ (Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam) and haṇa (Kannada).

Students complete the source analysis card individually, answering three structured questions: (1) What does the choice of motif on the Chalukya coin — Varaha and a royal parasol — suggest about what rulers wanted coins to communicate? (2) What does the find of Roman gold coins in Pudukkottai tell us about the reach of ancient Indian trade, and what are the limits of this evidence? (3) The word paṇa survives in four modern Indian languages — what does linguistic survival suggest about the depth and reach of the ancient monetary system?

Teacher facilitates a brief whole-class debrief on question two: what makes a coin a reliable historical source, and what can it not tell us? Students identify at least one strength and one limitation of coins as evidence. Teacher closes by noting that the alloys in modern Indian coins — iron, chromium, silicon, carbon — contrast sharply with the gold, silver, and copper of ancient coins, raising the question of what drives those material choices.

periods.section_context: Kārṣhāpaṇas, Chalukya and Chola coins, Roman gold coins Pudukkottai, paṇa linguistic lineage
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the broad monetary timeline, this unit goes deep into ancient coinage as a historical source — a methodologically distinct move that requires students to read objects as evidence rather than merely memorise names. Students frequently treat the Roman coin find as proof of Indian superiority rather than as evidence requiring interpretation; model the distinction between observation and inference carefully during the debrief. Source the coin images in advance — visual detail is essential to the analysis questions.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse ancient coins as historical sources to draw and evaluate inferences about trade, political authority, and inter-regional contact.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how minting authority and coin imagery functioned as instruments of trade facilitation and political legitimacy.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain contributions of Indian and global heritage to living cultural and economic traditions.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace the linguistic and symbolic heritage of ancient Indian coinage into contemporary Indian languages and monetary identity.

periods.activity_title: From Coins to Currency: The Rise of Paper Money in India
periods.section_anchor: The Journey of Money — Paper Money
materials: Printed image sheet: sample Indian currency notes showing cultural-heritage motifs on reverse, tactile identification marks
Short reading card: Bank of Bengal and Bank of Bombay context (80–100 words)
periods.visual_aids: Display of Indian currency note denominations: ₹10 through ₹500 (reverse side showing heritage motifs); annotation of tactile features

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses: 'Coins solved many barter problems — why would traders eventually stop relying on coins alone?' Students brainstorm in pairs for two minutes, then share. Teacher lists responses on the board; expected responses include weight, bulk, and security concerns. Teacher confirms that carrying large quantities of coins for high-value transactions became genuinely impractical as commercial activity scaled up.

Teacher narrates the development of paper money: first used in China; introduced in India in the late 18th century; early Indian notes issued by the Bank of Bengal and Bank of Bombay; while coins handled smaller denominations, paper currency served higher ones. Teacher displays the denomination list: coins at 50 paisa, ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10; notes at ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500, ₹1000. Contrast ancient individual rulers issuing coins with the modern arrangement: today the Reserve Bank of India is the sole legal authority to issue currency in India — no other entity may do so.

Students examine the printed image sheet of currency note reverses. Teacher draws attention to two design features: (1) cultural-heritage motifs on the reverse side — ask students to identify what specific heritage imagery they can see and what it communicates about India; (2) tactile identification marks — teacher explains these allow visually impaired persons to identify denominations by touch. Students write three sentences: one on what the heritage motifs communicate, one on what the tactile features reveal about design priorities, and one on why the RBI's sole authority to issue currency matters — what problem would arise if any entity could print notes.

Three or four students share their third sentence on RBI's exclusive authority. Teacher facilitates a brief whole-class response: what would happen to the value of money if anyone could issue currency? Students connect this to the unit-of-account function: a common denomination works only when supply is controlled. Teacher closes by asking students to name one way paper money solved a problem that coins could not.

periods.section_context: Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, RBI sole authority, denomination range, heritage motifs, tactile features
periods.teacher_notes: Having examined coins as objects of political and commercial significance, this unit traces why paper money emerged as the next practical necessity — a question of scale and portability rather than a simple technological upgrade. Students often assume the RBI has always issued currency; the colonial-era Bank of Bengal and Bank of Bombay provide important historical texture. The design features of notes — heritage motifs and tactile marks — are frequently overlooked details that reward close reading; bring physical or high-quality printed images.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how the transition from coins to paper currency responded to the practical demands of expanding trade and how institutional authority over currency evolved.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain why paper currency became necessary for high-value trade and how centralised issuing authority protects money's function as a unit of account.

periods.activity_title: Digital Money: How Payments Work Without Physical Currency
materials: Printed QR code image (large, scannable or illustrative)
periods.visual_aids: Projected or printed diagram: QR code → smartphone scan → bank account transfer flow

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Imagine a fruit seller at a roadside cart has no change for your ₹500 note. List every way the seller could still complete the sale.' Students brainstorm individually for two minutes. Collect responses: expected answers include digital payment, QR scan, UPI transfer. Teacher notes these on the board and tells students this unit will explain exactly how each method works.

Teacher explains digital money as money in electronic form that cannot be physically touched or felt. Define each form with its mechanism: debit cards and credit cards draw from or advance against bank accounts; net banking transfers funds via secure internet portals; UPI (Unified Payments Interface) links bank accounts directly for instant transfer. Display the QR code diagram: a QR code is a pattern of black and white squares encoding the receiver's bank account information; a smartphone or scanner reads it and initiates a direct account-to-account transfer. The fruit-seller example from the chapter: the cart displays a QR code, the customer scans it, and the payment goes directly into the seller's bank account — no physical currency changes hands.

Students write on their index card: three advantages of digital money compared to carrying paper currency (drawing on properties already discussed — portability, durability, ease of transaction) and two concerns or limitations a person might have about relying entirely on digital payments. Students share in pairs, then four or five read their concerns aloud.

Teacher facilitates structured analysis: Do digital payments solve all the problems the chapter has traced — double coincidence of wants, divisibility, portability, durability, store of value, deferred payment? Students work through the list aloud, deciding yes or no for each and giving a reason. Teacher closes by returning to the Keynes observation: does digital money 'link the present to the future' better than earlier forms, and in what new ways?

periods.section_context: Debit cards, credit cards, net banking, UPI, QR codes, account-to-account transfer, fruit-seller example
periods.teacher_notes: Having followed money's evolution from barter through coins and paper currency, students arrive at digital forms with enough conceptual vocabulary to evaluate them systematically — this unit should lean on that foundation rather than introduce digital payment as an entirely new topic. A common confusion is treating UPI and net banking as identical; the key distinction is that UPI enables instant inter-bank transfers without navigating a bank's own portal, which the QR diagram makes concrete. Prepare a large, clear QR code image — either projected or printed — before the sitting.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate digital payment mechanisms by applying the properties and functions of money established through earlier exchange systems.

periods.activity_title: Designing the Rupee: Heritage, Identity, and the ₹ Symbol
materials: Printed close-up image: ₹ symbol showing Devanagari 'Ra', Roman 'R', and the two parallel lines
periods.visual_aids: Enlarged annotated image of ₹ symbol: Devanagari Ra + Roman R + two horizontal lines (national flag / equal-to sign) labelled

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the ₹ symbol and asks: 'Before I explain its design, look carefully and describe every visual element you can see.' Students respond: two parallel lines at the top, a curved letter form. Teacher confirms the elements without explaining their meaning yet. Ask: 'Why would a government need a unique symbol for its currency, and what might it want the design to communicate?'

Teacher explains the design: the ₹ symbol was adopted by the Government of India in 2010, designed by Udaya Kumar of IIT Bombay. It combines the Devanagari letter 'Ra' (representing Indian script and languages) with the Roman 'R' (representing India's engagement with international commerce). The two horizontal parallel lines at the top carry dual symbolism — they echo the tricolour of the national flag and they replicate the mathematical 'equal to' sign, representing equality. Teacher connects this to the earlier note about the word paṇa surviving in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, and Kannada — the ₹ symbol is a contemporary moment in a long tradition of embedding identity into monetary objects, a tradition visible in Chalukya and Chola coin imagery.

Students design a hypothetical currency symbol for a fictional community, school, or region of their choosing. The symbol must intentionally combine at least two elements — one representing the community's heritage or values, and one representing its engagement with a wider world or economy — and students annotate the drawing with two or three sentences explaining what each element communicates and why they chose it.

Four or five students display and explain their symbol designs. Class identifies which design choices are most effective at communicating both elements simultaneously. Teacher closes by asking: 'From kārṣhāpaṇas with rūpas to the ₹ symbol — what remains constant in the way societies use monetary objects to express identity?'

periods.section_context: ₹ symbol design: Udaya Kumar, Devanagari Ra, Roman R, national flag parallel lines, 2010 adoption
pedagogical_approaches: Some specific opportunities for projects to create models and artefacts
periods.teacher_notes: Having studied coinage as historical evidence, this unit extends that analytical lens to a contemporary design object — the ₹ symbol — connecting the ancient practice of embedding identity in monetary objects to a 2010 government decision. Students sometimes focus exclusively on the aesthetic aspects of their symbol design; redirect them to the deliberate communicative logic of each element, mirroring the analysis they applied to Chalukya and Chola coin motifs. The annotated drawing is completed and discussed within this sitting; no extension outside the unit is needed.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain contributions of Indian and global heritage to living cultural and economic traditions.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how the ₹ symbol design synthesises Indian and global heritage elements and connects to a longer tradition of monetary identity.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace continuity in the practice of encoding political and cultural identity into monetary objects from ancient coinage to contemporary symbol design.

periods.activity_title: Barter to Digital: A Structured Whole-Chapter Comparison
periods.section_anchor: Barter System / Why Do We Need Money? — Problems of the Barter System / Basic Functions of Money / New Forms of Money
materials: A3 paper or two joined notebook pages per group of three

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the anchoring question: 'If you had to advise a community that currently uses only barter on whether to adopt digital money directly — skipping coins and paper — what would you need to know and what would you argue?' Students write one paragraph individually in response, drawing on the full range of exchange forms the chapter covers.

Groups of three construct a comparison table on A3 paper. Columns: Barter | Commodity Money | Metal Coins | Paper Currency | Digital Money. Rows: Solves double coincidence (yes/no/partial) | Divisible | Portable | Durable | Store of value | Requires institutional authority | Needs literacy or technology. Groups complete the table using the chapter's content, marking each cell and adding a brief note where the answer is partial.

Each group reviews their table and writes a three-sentence recommendation responding to the opening question: should the community skip directly to digital money, and what two conditions would have to be in place for that to work? The recommendation must cite at least two rows from their comparison table as evidence.

Three groups read their recommendations aloud. Class identifies where groups' conditions agree and where they differ. Teacher closes by noting that the chapter's entire arc — from the Junbeel Mela to QR codes — is captured in the rows of the table students just built.

periods.section_context: Comparison of barter, commodity money, coinage, paper currency, digital money across key economic properties
periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the full span of exchange forms the chapter covers, asking students to apply the analytical vocabulary built across the chapter to a structured evaluative task — the comparison table format makes the reasoning visible and the recommendation testable. A common weakness in the recommendation is listing features rather than making a conditional argument; require students to name the conditions explicitly. Groups build the table and write the recommendation within this sitting; nothing prepared beforehand is needed.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the relative merits of different exchange systems by applying economic properties across a structured comparison.

periods.activity_title: Money, Society, and Change: A Reflective Essay on Monetary Evolution
periods.section_anchor: The Journey of Money / The Journey of Money — Coinage / The Journey of Money — Paper Money / New Forms of Money

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the essay prompt on the board: 'The story of money is the story of how societies solved problems and created new ones. Using at least three specific examples from India's monetary history, explain how each transition in the journey of money both addressed an earlier limitation and introduced a new challenge or requirement.' Teacher reads the prompt aloud and unpacks it: 'specific examples' means named objects, institutions, or events; 'transition' means the shift from one form to the next; 'new challenge or requirement' means something the new form demands that the old one did not.

Students plan their essay on a half-sheet: list their three chosen transitions and for each, note the old limitation solved and the new challenge created. Teacher circulates and checks that each planned example is specific — 'coinage' alone is too vague; 'kārṣhāpaṇas replacing cowries' or 'RBI replacing Bank of Bengal note issue' is specific. Teacher also checks that each 'new challenge' is genuinely a challenge introduced by the new form, not simply a description of how it works.

Students write their essay. The scaffold on the board guides structure: Paragraph 1 — introduce the chapter's central question (how exchange systems evolved); Paragraphs 2–4 — one transition each, with the limitation solved and challenge introduced; Paragraph 5 — a closing reflection on whether the evolution of money is primarily driven by solving problems or by social and institutional change. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are writing description without analysis.

Two or three students read their closing reflection paragraph aloud. Class responds to each with one agreement and one pushback. Teacher closes by returning to the Keynes framing: 'money links the present to the future' — ask students whether this is equally true of barter, coins, and digital money, or whether some forms of money link the present to the future more powerfully than others.

periods.section_context: India's monetary transitions: kārṣhāpaṇas, paper currency, RBI authority, digital payments as sequential problem-solutions
periods.teacher_notes: Having built analytical vocabulary and comparison frameworks across the chapter, students are positioned here to synthesise — to construct an argument about monetary evolution rather than narrate it. The most common weakness in this essay is treating each transition as purely progressive (each form is simply better); push students to articulate the genuine new demands each form creates — RBI authority requires a functioning legal system; digital money requires literacy, device access, and connectivity. Plan and draft are both completed within this sitting.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare the practical properties of different commodity-exchange objects to evaluate their suitability as media of exchange.
assessment_items.question_text: A community on a remote island uses large stone discs as a medium of exchange. A trader wants to use these stones to buy fish at a market three villages away. Which property of these stones makes them LEAST suitable for this transaction?

options.label: A
options.text: They are scarce and hard to find in the region.

options.label: B
options.text: They cannot be transported easily from one place to another.

options.label: C
options.text: They are not accepted by the sellers in distant markets.

options.label: D
options.text: They deteriorate quickly in humid coastal climates.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses scarcity (which can make an object valuable) with portability; the student has not separated the property being tested from general value judgements.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses acceptance (which depends on trust and familiarity) with the physical property of portability; acceptance is a separate issue from moving the object.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misidentifies the problem as durability rather than portability; stone does not deteriorate, so this distractor surfaces a confusion between two different barter problems.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate digital payment mechanisms by applying the properties and functions of money established through earlier exchange systems.
assessment_items.question_text: A street vendor displays a QR code on her cart. A customer scans it and pays ₹50 for vegetables. Which property of money does this digital transaction demonstrate MOST clearly when compared with paying by handing over a coin?

options.label: A
options.text: Standard of deferred payment, because the vendor will receive the money only after clearing by the bank.

options.label: B
options.text: Store of value, because digital money does not deteriorate the way metal coins rust over time.

options.label: C
options.text: Portability, because neither the buyer nor the seller needs to carry physical currency for the transaction.

options.label: D
options.text: Divisibility, because digital systems can break any amount into exact paisa without rounding.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students unfamiliar with digital payment from personal experience may need a brief verbal description of the QR scan process before answering; this does not affect the cognitive demand.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses 'deferred payment' (paying later) with bank processing delay; the student does not understand that UPI transfers are near-instant and that deferred payment refers to a deliberate future obligation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies the store-of-value function incorrectly; the comparison is between the transaction mechanism, not long-term storage, and metal coins do not typically rust in the way described.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Divisibility is a genuine property of digital money but it is not what the QR scenario foregrounds; this distractor reveals a student who can recall functions but cannot select the most relevant one for the specific scenario.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can diagnose the structural limitations of barter exchange by applying named economic problems to a concrete trade scenario.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Why Do We Need Money? — Problems of the Barter System
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. The table shows three traders and what they own and need. For each trader, identify the specific barter problem illustrated and explain in one sentence why that problem makes the exchange difficult.
expected_elements: Trader 1: identifies the problem of double coincidence of wants — Priya needs someone who both wants fish AND has rice to offer; finding a perfect two-way match is rare.
Trader 2: identifies the problem of divisibility — a live goat cannot be split into portions to purchase three separate small items (a knife, salt, and cloth).
Trader 3: identifies the problem of durability — mangoes rot within days, so they cannot be saved and used as payment at a later time.
assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Trader | Owns | Needs
Priya | Extra fish | A bag of rice
Ramu | One goat | A knife, a bag of salt, and a piece of cloth
Leela | A basket of ripe mangoes | Medicines (to be paid for next week)
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may respond in bullet points rather than full sentences if sentence construction is a barrier; the cognitive task is identification and explanation, not writing form.

expected_elements: Trader 1: names double coincidence of wants and explains that Priya must find someone who both wants fish and has rice — two conditions must be met simultaneously.
Trader 2: names divisibility and explains that a whole goat cannot be broken into three parts to pay for three separate small items.
Trader 3: names durability and explains that ripe mangoes will rot before next week's payment is due, making them unsuitable as a deferred payment medium.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the relative merits of different exchange systems by applying economic properties across a structured comparison.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Barter System / Why Do We Need Money? — Problems of the Barter System / Basic Functions of Money / New Forms of Money
assessment_items.question_text: A historian argues: 'Each new form of money in history solved one problem but created a new requirement that the previous form never had.' Using at least two specific transitions from the history of money (for example, from barter to coinage, or from coins to paper currency, or from paper currency to digital money), evaluate this argument. Do you agree, partly agree, or disagree? Justify your position with evidence from the chapter.
look_for: Identifies at least two specific transitions with accurate content (e.g., barter to coinage resolves divisibility and portability but requires minting authority and ruler acceptance; coins to paper currency resolves bulk portability but requires a central issuing institution such as the Bank of Bengal or RBI; paper to digital resolves physical portability but requires device access, literacy, and banking infrastructure).
Articulates both what the new form solved AND what new requirement it introduced for each chosen transition — not merely describing the form.
Takes a clear position (agree / partly agree / disagree) and applies it consistently to both transitions rather than listing features without evaluating the claim.
Uses chapter-specific evidence: named institutions (RBI, Bank of Bengal), specific barter problems (divisibility, durability, double coincidence), or named forms (kārṣhāpaṇas, UPI, QR codes).
Avoids treating each transition as purely progressive — acknowledges that each advance introduces a genuine new demand on society or infrastructure.
Names at least two transitions accurately and identifies both the problem solved and the new requirement introduced for each.
Takes and sustains an evaluative position rather than simply describing forms of money.
Draws on chapter-specific content — named institutions, barter problems by name, or specific monetary forms.
Recognises that 'new requirement' is not a flaw but a social or institutional condition the new form depends on.
Maintains internal consistency: the position taken (agree/partly agree/disagree) is supported by, not contradicted by, the examples chosen.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse the key elements of trade and commerce, including how commodity exchange and money evolved to facilitate production, consumption, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct an evidence-based argument about the driving forces behind monetary evolution using specific examples from India's economic history.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Journey of Money / The Journey of Money — Coinage / The Journey of Money — Paper Money / New Forms of Money
assessment_items.task: You are preparing a display panel titled 'Why Did Money Keep Changing?' for a school exhibition on economic history. Create a cause-effect map that shows at least three transitions in the history of money — from barter through to a form used today — where each arrow represents a cause (what problem or limitation drove the change) and each new box represents the effect (the new form of money that emerged). Below the map, write three sentences: one naming the transition you find most significant, one explaining your reason using evidence from the chapter, and one identifying a new requirement that the form of money you chose introduced.
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1: Draw your first box and label it with the earliest form of money you will include (e.g., barter or cowrie shells). Step 2: Draw an arrow leading to the next box and label the arrow with the specific problem that drove the transition (e.g., 'goods rot — durability problem'). Step 3: Label the new box with the next form of money. Step 4: Repeat for at least two more transitions. Step 5: Review — does each arrow name a cause drawn from the chapter? Does each box name a specific form? Step 6: Write your three sentences below the map.
format_of_output: A hand-drawn cause-effect map with at least three labelled boxes and labelled arrows, completed on paper
Three written sentences below the map as specified in the task
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may label their map in their home language and write the sentences in any language the teacher can read; the analytical demand — identifying causes and effects — is not language-dependent.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students construct an original causal argument about monetary evolution, selecting and sequencing evidence from across the chapter to explain what drove each transition — demonstrating Evaluation-level thinking about economic change.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The six-step scaffold guides students through the map before the sentences; Step 5 (review) is critical — check that each arrow names a cause from the chapter, not a feature of the new form. The three sentences require the student to single out the most significant transition and justify it with evidence, which is the evaluative core of the task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: transitions are accurately labelled with named causes (specific barter problems or named practical limitations); arrows carry precise causal language rather than vague descriptions; the three sentences name a specific transition, cite a piece of chapter evidence, and name a genuine new requirement. Weak: boxes are labelled without arrows, or arrows are labelled with descriptions of the new form rather than causes; the three sentences summarise the map rather than evaluating it; no chapter-specific evidence appears.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle for an LO asking students to construct an argument about driving forces — it makes causal reasoning visible and structured, directly mirroring how the chapter organises its explanation of monetary evolution. The teacher may substitute any other format from the Open Task menu.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse ancient coins as historical sources to draw and evaluate inferences about trade, political authority, and inter-regional contact.
assessment_items.question_text: Roman gold coins were excavated at Pudukkottai in Tamil Nadu. A historian uses this find to argue that ancient India engaged in maritime trade with Rome and that this trade favoured India. Which statement BEST explains WHY the find of Roman gold coins in India supports the claim that trade favoured India?

options.label: A
options.text: Roman coins are made of gold, which proves that Rome was richer than ancient Indian kingdoms.

options.label: B
options.text: Roman coins ending up in India suggests Romans paid for Indian goods with gold, meaning India was a net exporter and accumulated Roman currency.

options.label: C
options.text: The presence of foreign coins in India shows that Indian rulers accepted many types of currency for taxation.

options.label: D
options.text: Finding Roman coins confirms that Roman merchants lived permanently in Tamil Nadu and ran businesses there.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the material value of a coin with the trade balance; the student does not understand that finding foreign gold coins in India implies payment flowing INTO India, not that Rome was wealthier.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces taxation, which is not what the find or the chapter's argument is about; reveals a student who has connected coins to state authority but not to trade balance.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Moves from 'coins found here' to 'people lived here permanently' — an overclaim the evidence does not support; reveals a student who cannot distinguish between evidence of contact and evidence of settlement.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct an analytical argument about how successive monetary transitions both resolved prior limitations and generated new social or institutional requirements.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Journey of Money / The Journey of Money — Coinage / The Journey of Money — Paper Money / New Forms of Money
assessment_items.question_text: In ancient India, individual rulers issued coins. Today, only the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may legally issue currency. Which statement BEST explains why centralising this authority in the RBI matters for the economy?

options.label: A
options.text: It prevents coins from being made of rare metals, which keeps the cost of production low.

options.label: B
options.text: It ensures that only one design of currency note is printed, making notes easier to recognise.

options.label: C
options.text: It controls the supply of money so that its value as a common unit of account remains stable and trustworthy.

options.label: D
options.text: It stops foreign currencies from entering India and competing with the rupee.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses centralised authority with decisions about coin material; a student who recalls that ancient coins used precious metals but has not connected the RBI's role to the unit-of-account function.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reduces centralised authority to a design-standardisation issue, missing the economic rationale; the student identifies a surface consequence (uniform design) rather than the underlying economic purpose.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces foreign currency competition, which is not what the chapter discusses in relation to RBI's currency authority; reveals a student conflating monetary sovereignty with trade policy.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how the transition from coins to paper currency responded to the practical demands of expanding trade and how institutional authority over currency evolved.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Journey of Money — Paper Money
assessment_items.question_text: Explain TWO reasons why paper money became necessary as trade expanded, and name ONE institution that issued early paper currency in India before the Reserve Bank of India took over this role.
expected_elements: First reason: carrying and storing large quantities of coins became impractical as the volume and value of transactions grew — bulk and weight made high-value trade cumbersome.
Second reason: coins were suited to smaller denominations but could not efficiently serve high-value transactions; paper currency served those higher denominations.
Named institution: Bank of Bengal OR Bank of Bombay (either is correct).
Provides two distinct reasons — both must be genuinely about why paper money was needed, not simply descriptions of how paper money works.
Names at least one of: Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay.
Does not conflate the two reasons into a single point about weight/bulk.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how the Junbeel Mela represents a living Indian heritage practice that combines socio-cultural and economic exchange.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Why Do We Need Money? — Continuing Barter Practices
assessment_items.question_text: The Junbeel Mela, held in Morigaon district of Assam, is described in the chapter as a living example of barter. Which statement BEST describes what makes the Junbeel Mela significant beyond being simply a trading fair?

options.label: A
options.text: It is the only place in India where barter is still legally permitted.

options.label: B
options.text: It began as a gathering for political discussion among tribal chiefs and evolved into a space for community exchange of goods unavailable across ecological zones.

options.label: C
options.text: It allows hill communities to sell goods at prices higher than those available in city markets.

options.label: D
options.text: It was established by the Government of Assam in the 20th century to preserve tribal customs.

what_each_option_reveals.A: A fabricated legal claim not in the chapter; a student who has understood that barter is unusual but has not read the actual chapter content carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reduces the Mela to a price-advantage trade fair, ignoring its socio-cultural and political heritage; a student who has focused only on the exchange-of-goods aspect.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Contradicts the chapter's explicit statement that the fair dates to the 15th century and originates in tribal community practice; a student who has confused the historical origin with a modern government initiative.

competency.competency_text: Identify and explain contributions of Indian and global heritage to living cultural and economic traditions.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how the ₹ symbol design synthesises Indian and global heritage elements and connects to a longer tradition of monetary identity.
assessment_items.question_text: The ₹ symbol, adopted by India in 2010, combines the Devanagari letter 'Ra' and the Roman letter 'R', with two parallel horizontal lines at the top. Which statement BEST explains what the design of the ₹ symbol communicates about India's monetary identity?

options.label: A
options.text: It signals that India accepts only Devanagari script in all official financial transactions.

options.label: B
options.text: It represents India's intention to replace the Roman alphabet with Devanagari in international trade.

options.label: C
options.text: It combines Indian linguistic heritage with international readability, while the two lines evoke both the national flag and a sign of equality.

options.label: D
options.text: It was designed to make the rupee look similar to the euro symbol so that foreign traders would find it familiar.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Over-reads the Devanagari element as a policy statement about script exclusivity; a student who has noticed the Devanagari Ra but has not understood the dual-heritage logic of the design.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Misreads the inclusion of the Roman R as a competitive or replacement gesture rather than an integrative one; a student who has not understood that both scripts appear together intentionally.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fabricates a comparison with the euro that does not appear in the chapter; a student who has latched onto 'international' as a concept but introduced content from outside the chapter.
